content.thinking:
I need to write the whole module carefully in one pass without typechecking, using a plain-object prop group where joints only apply to moving parts, and I'm figuring out whether a rigid part without a bone still needs a root joint created by default.

I'll explicitly create a "root" joint at the origin for static parts, plus a "lidHinge" joint parented to root for the chest lid so it can swing open. I'm planning the overall layout: a stone flagstone slab as the base floor patch sized around 2.2 x 1.8 meters with a small thickness, positioning everything to stand just above it, and setting up a small texel size with stone and wood textures for the surfaces.

Rather than tiling one giant floor slab (which would make the stone texture too chunky), I'm switching to building the floor from a grid of individual flagstone boxes, each sized so its top face divides evenly into texel units for a crisp stone pattern.

I'm laying out a 5x4 grid of tiles with small gaps between them, varying heights slightly, over a darker grout slab underneath to sell the look of individual stones.

Next I'm building a wooden chest: a boxy body with wood texturing, reinforced by vertical iron bands made from slightly larger boxes, and a curved lid formed from a half-cylinder rotated so its axis runs sideways, giving a domed top that faces upward.

I'm adding a gold lock plate with keyhole texture, corner studs, and side handles, plus some spilled gold coins and a gem in front of the chest. I'm also working out the hinge rotation math to pose the lid slightly open, figuring out which axis direction and sign gives the front edge lifting upward rather than closing further.

With the lid open, I'm building an interior gold heap using stacked boxes of decreasing size textured like coins, topped with cylinder coins and gems, so the inside reads as a treasure pile rather than an empty shell. Now I'm moving on to planning a standing brazier-style torch prop for the next piece of the scene.

Now I'm designing the torch stands themselves — stone pedestal base, wooden pole, cloth-wrapped head, and iron cage rods topped with the flame, placed in the back corners away from the chest. I'm also planning a fallen, charred torch lying on the floor with a rotated pole and head plus a few glowing ember specks scattered nearby.

For the barrels, I'm setting up a lathe profile to shape an octagonal wooden barrel with a bulging silhouette, then using cell painting to color individual staves by their angular position and add iron hoop bands at specific height ranges.

Still computing barrel profile...

I'm thinking about giving one barrel an open top revealing dark liquid for visual interest, while keeping the other barrel simply closed to avoid overcomplicating the scene.

Writing the lathe profile coordinates...

Still shaping the cylinder cap...

For the barrel lying on its side, I can reuse the same lathe outline but rotate the axis to [1,0,0] instead of the default vertical axis.

I'll settle the barrel's floor intersection as acceptable since it's within the model's lowest-point tolerance, then add wedge-shaped chocks to cradle the lying barrel for support. Next I'm moving on to the bone pile — planning a skull, ribcage, femurs, and vertebrae, starting with femurs as rods with knobbed ends.

Designing bone geometry...

I need to work out texel resolution so painted details stay crisp: estimating total painted surface area across barrels and bones, I'm sizing the paint sheet to around 2048px with cell sizes tuned so each paint cell covers several texels. Then I'm starting on the skull shape as a cranium box with a simple front-face texture for eyes.

I'm planning the skull's eye sockets, nose, and teeth as separate small dark boxes slightly protruding from the face, with teeth either merged into one box geometry or drawn as a simple pixel-art textured plane for simplicity.

Now I'm working out how to rotate each skull part around the overall skull center rather than its own local origin, so I'll write a helper function that applies a yaw rotation to each part's position before placing it.

For the ribcage, I'm planning vertebrae as a stacked column of boxes with ribs built as short polyline rods curving outward from each spine point, keeping a blocky pixel-art look rather than smooth sweeps.

Still shaping the ribs...

For the rest of the scene, I'm planning skull, ribcage, three femurs, a few small vertebrae, finger bones, and adding an iron manacle with chain links made from small ring-like box approximations near the bones.

For the spike trap, I'm designing a recessed pressure plate with a darker stone border frame, a dark inner pit, and a 5x5 grid of pyramid-style spikes—steel gray with lighter tips, mostly extended but with one corner broken or shorter, and a rusty bloodied tip for detail.

I'll paint the spikes using height-based gradients: a steel ramp for most of the cone and a darker, bloody red near the tip based on relative height above the base, giving each spike a worn, menacing look. I'm also planning pressure tiles near the trap, possibly marked with skull imagery for warning.

Now I'm working through the exact positioning of trap elements and furniture on the floor — torches, chest, barrels — making sure nothing overlaps by checking their spans in x and z and adjusting positions where they'd collide.

Now I'm placing lying skeleton remains near (-0.82,0.35) with a skull by the trap edge, plus a second bone cluster further along the pit. I'm also thinking about adding moss patches as thin green floor boxes and a cobweb card tucked into a corner for extra detail.

I'm sketching small debris like pebbles, mossy clumps, and scattered coins near the chest, deciding against glow effects but keeping torch embers for atmosphere. I'm settling on model and torch heights around 1.3m and 1.25m respectively, and capping the color palette at roughly 64 flat colors for flames and gold accents.

Now I'm writing the stone tile texture function, defining a grayscale ramp and dithering the fill pattern across a 32x32 tile using a seeded RNG.

Still writing tile textures...

I'm figuring out texel sizes for wood and stone so planks and bricks tile cleanly without stretching, then working out the iron band texture dimensions so rivets and band faces line up at a consistent scale across the chest lid and body.

Then for the top face crop size I settle on 6x32, and move to the gold coin tile: a 16x16 dithered yellow ramp with a 4x4 coin pattern stamped on top for texture.

I work out texel sizing for tile boxes, adjusting to 0.0275 then settling on a 48x48 gold tile so the math divides cleanly. Next I design a small keyhole lock plate texture with a gold border and dark keyhole, placed as a textured plane with a fine 0.01 texel, then start sketching a skull face texture with eye sockets.

Rather than building the skull from separate parts, I decide a single pixel-art decal across the cranium front makes more sense: a bone-colored base with dark socket holes. I split the skull into a cranium box and a jaw box, planning to fill all faces with a dithered bone-color ramp and stamp dark eye sockets and a nose shape on the cranium's front face, plus a teeth row on the jaw front, using a shared skin layout sized to fit both pieces.

Writing skull texture code...

Adding upper teeth row, then setting the skinBox texel scale to convert cranium dimensions (16×12×16) into actual block units for the skin faces.

Now I'm positioning the jaw box beneath and in front of the cranium, keeping yaw-only rotation so the skull sits upright on the floor without tilting on other axes.

Adjusting jaw forward offset to align flush with the cranium's front edge, then adding small zygomatic cheek boxes on the sides and considering a slight tilt rotation for the skull.

I'll simplify by only applying a cranium tilt back for expression rather than rotating every part, and assign the skull a white texture. For torch details I'm planning to use a wood-textured pole and a small tiled cloth wrap with stripes, leaning on cellPaint coloring for minor items to keep the texture atlas small, and I'm sketching out a flame helper function defining row widths for the outer flame shape.

Defining flame layer spans...

Still defining torch dimensions...

Now I'm sketching the pit trap structure near tx=-0.15, tz=0.38, starting with the stone border frame made of four boxes.

Still building spike trap geometry...

I'm tallying total part counts across floor, chest, torches, barrels, bones, and the trap to stay under budget, and considering merging the 25 collar boxes into a single geometry using mergeGeometries to cut down on object count.

I'll skip adding a pressure plate, lever, or warning sign since reliance on tile textures covers that need, and I'm keeping the prop list focused on chest, torches, barrels, bones, and the spike trap plus small details like coins and webs. Now I'm sketching out the barrel function's options for position, openness, and orientation.

Defining the barrel lathe profile...

Adding hoop coloring and wood stave paint logic...

I realize the seam is sampled per-texel rather than per-cell, so a 2.5° seam could get aliased at this resolution. I need to compute the stave angle from the actual texel position relative to the barrel axis instead of relying on the cell's interpolated coordinate, so the seams stay crisp regardless of orientation.

For end caps on lying barrels, I'll use planks with a different axis for the pattern. I'm also planning extra details: a spigot on barrel A, cradle chocks for the lying barrel, and a small pixel-art poison/skull label painted on barrel A's surface.

Rather than fuss over exact placement geometry on the curved octagonal barrel, I realize the cleaner approach is using a decal function that projects the label texture directly onto the barrel's surface at a given point and direction, avoiding floating or intersecting planes.

For the bone material, I'm setting up a cell-based paint with a tan-to-cream color ramp driven by surface normal and some dithered randomness, plus a noise check for mould staining.

Now I'm designing a bone-rod helper that builds a shaft box between two points plus knob boxes at each end, computing a perpendicular vector via cross product with the Y-axis to offset and orient the knobs, with a fallback axis if the direction is vertical.

Then I'm planning the femur's heavier knob ends and a vertebrae chain made of small boxes arranged along a curve with tiny spinal process spikes, feeding into a ribcage structure where ribs extend sideways from a spine running along the local x-axis.

I'm working out ribs as swept tapered tubes with rounded caps, and building a placer function that rotates coordinates around the Y axis using standard Euler rotation math so each body part can be positioned and oriented consistently, including computing proper global directions for rod-like parts that need a direction vector.

Now I'm planning the rib cage curvature with five paired ribs scaling in length, adding small finger bones, and designing a manacle-and-chain detail using torus geometry for both the ring and a short chain of alternating flat and edge-on links.

I'm figuring out the vertical positioning so links sit correctly relative to the floor height, with cuffs rendered as thicker torus shapes and an iron-toned paint ramp with rust speckling for the color. I'm also considering whether floor tiles should have slight height variation rather than a fixed 0.06 value.

Now I'm adding small environmental details like green moss patches scattered near torches and barrels, scrapping the idea of cobwebs since there's no wall surface to anchor them, and starting to enumerate the chest's positioning and features.

I'm working through the chest's rotation, giving it a slight 10° yaw for a storybook feel, which means recalculating the hinge axis for the lid so it still swings correctly relative to the chest's rotated local space.

Now I'm placing the chest body as a tiled wooden box, then adding a dark interior panel just above its top face, and stacking smaller gold heap boxes on top to suggest a pile of treasure spilling out.

I'm also scattering around a dozen small tilted cylinder "coins" randomly across the heap, rotating and translating each before merging them all into one geometry so they share consistent attributes with the boxes, then applying a flat gold color.

Next I'm adding gem accents — three glowing octahedrons in red, blue, and green scattered on the heap — followed by vertical iron corner straps on the chest body, making sure the bands only wrap the front/back/sides and leave the top opening clear.

I realize the metal texture would get too stretched across the large faces, so I'll skip the iron texture entirely and use simple paint for the straps and bands instead. For rivets, I'm placing small merged cube clusters along the front straps at a few height intervals to simulate bolted details.

Now I'm working out the lid's layered arch structure — stacking progressively narrower wood bands by depth and height, sizing the wood texture tiles so they fit evenly across the 0.52 width, and planning paired iron straps running over the arch at symmetric x positions, skipping curved end caps for simplicity.

I'm also placing a gold lock plate on the front of the body and an iron hasp strap on the lid's front face, then setting up the hinge joint at the back-top edge with a rod-like iron barrel and simple knuckle boxes, with the lid's rotation posed around that hinge axis.

Checking the 38° lid-opening angle: since the hinge sits right at the body's back-top edge, the lid rotates cleanly around that line, with the rear staying put and the front rising — though I need to verify the lid doesn't clip into the gold heap near the front as it swings up.

To fix that, I'll shift the heap depth forward so it's centered off the hinge axis, shrinking both tiers so the back edge clears the lid curve safely.

I'm also sketching out a pixel-art warning label design — a skull motif on a red background using a small color palette.

Still sketching the skull rows...

Now I'm setting up a charred fallen torch prop using a wood pole with blackened embers, then starting the builder code with a root joint and a couple of seeded random generators, trying to stay careful about unused variables under strict typechecking.

Writing box helper and type imports...

Still writing placer and helper logic...

Checking which imports I actually need—keeping pick, bayer, stepped, skinBox, skinLayout, and pixelArt since they're used, then setting up the meta block and defining the stone color palette for texture generation.

Writing stone texture code...

Writing wood texture generator...

Still designing pixel textures...

Now I'm setting up wood and barrel color palettes, planning a barrel-painting function that handles cell-based rendering with different material variants like iron bands.

Still writing barrel geometry logic...

I'm adding seam darkening and random streaks along the stave direction, then normalizing with the wood palette lookup. There's a lingering concern about whether the 45° angle bins actually line up with the octagonal facet corners, but I decide the misalignment is minor and will still look like acceptable plank seams for the pixel-art style, so I leave the phase offset at zero.

Now I'm defining the iron paint for the barrel interior using noise to scatter rust patches against the base iron ramp, and sketching a shared spike-paint function that ramps steel color by height with optional blood staining near the tip. To avoid baking a separate paint per spike, I'm consolidating into three shared paints — plain steel, bloodied steel, and rusted steel — each using a constant base ramp.

I'm laying out the spike grid positions and heights, varying them slightly per spike with some shorter or broken stumps, and rotating the cone geometries 45 degrees so their four-sided faces align better. Now I'm starting to write the bone rod function for the skeleton prop.

Still writing bone part logic...

Skipping the sternum and keeping the pelvis as two simple boxes, I'm now setting up the skull placement using the placer's rotation, building the cranium from the base skin box shape.

I'm positioning the jaw and cranium so they overlap correctly, computing the cranium's vertical center so it rests just above the jaw and their front faces align closely.

I'm fleshing out the skinbox textures, making sure every face rectangle for both boxes gets filled with the ramp color, then moving on to building the torch function with a tiled stone base and starting a second tier.

For the torch pole, I'm calculating dimensions so the wood texture tiling matches cleanly, resizing the wood texture to 40x60 with plank rows to avoid mismatched texel sizes against the pole's face dimensions.

Rather than horizontal plank bands that'd look like stacked logs on a vertical pole, I'm switching to a cell-painting approach for vertical wood grain streaks, trying to seed the randomness by column position so the streaks run lengthwise along the pole instead of around it.

Settling on using noise sampled from the flattened x/z position for the grain pattern, plus knot details, then painting with the pole color. For the chest I'm adding textured planks, iron collar bands as small boxes near the base and top, a cloth-wrapped head section, and a flared cap above it, then starting on cage rods running from near the base up to the flare.

Now I'm sketching a thin ring frame from four small boxes to close the top of the cage, placing a flame shape inside sized to fit the model's height, and adding a few tiny ember cubes scattered near the base -- while deciding to skip a separate glowing floor decal since it would require retexturing the tile itself.

For the fallen torch, I'm positioning a rotated pole piece with wood-grained paint, a charred head block at its end, iron collar details, and scattered ember glow specks, plus reusing the flame function at a smaller scale to suggest a still-smoldering remnant.

Now I'm adding a slime puddle beneath barrel B as a thin glowing green box, rubble rocks with randomized rotation and stone-colored dithered paint, and moss patch boxes scattered near torch bases and barrels, carefully positioned to sit just above the floor tile surface without clipping.

I'm also planning a glowing rune warning plate in front of the trap tile: a flat plane rotated to face upward, textured with a small pixel-art red rune symbol like a warning X-in-box design, given a subtle glow effect to make it feel ominous and ritualistic.

Adjusting trap and chest placement to avoid overlap...

Now I'm working out the skeleton remains position, checking the trap x-range and ribcage center/orientation to fit within the scene bounds.

I'm placing the crossed femurs and skull with a slight yaw, then checking for overlaps with the barrel near x 0.45-1.05, so I'm shifting the manacle chain to a clearer spot around (-0.3, 0.9).

Now I'm positioning the fallen torch in the front-right region, calculating its extent along the rotated yaw axis so it spans roughly x 0.27-0.97 at z≈0.5, then figuring out where to run the chain along x at z 0.82 without colliding with it.

I'll place the right femur nearby at (0.9,0.68) with a slight tilt, accepting minor overlaps near the box since they won't be visually significant, and skip loose bones near barrel B for now. Then I shift to defining the barrel lid's hinge joint, setting up its rotation axis and attachment point so it can swing open at the right angle.

Finally I turn to scattering coins around the chest—mixing lying and leaning coins near the front local coordinates to make the pile look natural and merged.

I'm sorting out part counts and merge groups: gold heap textured within texel limits, additional coins merged into the heap, rivets and studs along the lid edges, and a helper function to transform geometry into world space with rotation and translation for each piece.

Setting up the builder, RNG seeds, and palette definitions...

I'm working out rotation ordering, deciding to mostly just use yaw around Y for simplicity rather than combining tilts, then setting up a textured box helper variant for tiled surfaces.

Now I'm laying out the floor: adding a flat base slab, then computing a grid of positions for tiles across the floor with spacing and gaps between rows and columns.

Still writing floor tiles...

I'm also setting up the chest geometry, placing it with a slight yaw rotation and defining its body dimensions and texture.

Still writing chest details...

Positioning the hasp and lock plate pieces...

Adding merged strap studs with muted gray color, then moving on to building torch, barrel, trap, and debris functions, starting with a flame shape built from layered stepped outlines for its core, mid, and outer layers.

Still writing flame logic...

I'm defining an ember-spark helper that scatters small glowing boxes above a point, then starting the spike trap construction with a stone frame built from front/back and side boxes around a placed anchor point.

Now I'm figuring out the inner opening size and switching to a cell-painted stone material with edge highlighting and random cracks for the frame texture, then positioning the frame's top face and adding a rusted plate box beneath it.

Working out the plate, holes, and collar geometry with merged boxes for performance, then placing dark spike cones centered above the collar base with no yaw rotation on the frames.

I'm deciding to skip extra flourishes like skull decals or bones on the spikes to keep things simple, then moving on to writing the color palette constants and paint helper functions with proper TypeScript typing for the cell callback.

Still writing palette colors...

Still defining cloth and character color palettes, then adding ember-glow cells for the fallen head and setting up the pole paint function...

I need two separate noise orientations for the pole wood grain—one stretched along y for standing poles, one along a different axis for fallen ones—since world-space streaking would look wrong if I apply the same grain direction regardless of rotation.

Checking tile dimensions against pole size confirms the fallen pole's wood texture maps cleanly with planks running horizontal across its length, giving correct grain direction. For the standing pole, I'll apply the same tiled box texture but need the plank rows to form cross-grain bands instead.

Now I'm defining a barrel function that computes radius as a function of height for the barrel's bulge, handles both upright and lying orientations with a yaw rotation, and sets up the center position and directional axis accordingly.

Still working out log angle logic...

For the barrel shape, I'm defining the cross-section as a lathe profile: a series of radius samples along the height, starting and ending at the axis, which the lathe operation can revolve into a full barrel form with hoop bands.

Checking the hoop radius sizing to make sure it covers the octagon barrel's apothem properly, and confirming the hoop lathe outline shares the same axis origin as the barrel so positions line up. Then I'm setting up a decal label placement on the standing barrel with its position, direction, and size.

For barrel extras, I'm adding a small iron spigot pipe box and brass faucet handle near the front-lower face of barrel A. For the open barrel B, I'm adding a glowing green liquid disc near the top plus some bubbles, while deciding to skip extra details like a resting ladle or bones to keep things simple.

For the cradle C, I'm placing small wedge-shaped wood chocks beside the barrel ends to keep it from rolling, positioning them laterally near the base.

Now writing the full generation code: cone-shaped trap spikes with colors varying by position (rust for broken stumps, blood-red for armed spikes), plus debris scattering and the final lid pose applied after all parts are assembled on the hinge. I'm also setting up the skull's texture layout with cranium and jaw dimensions for painting detail sheets.

Painting the skull face: filling bone-colored base tones with dithering, then stamping dark eye sockets, a nose cavity, and rows of upper teeth in cream and dark outline colors onto the cranium's front face, followed by starting the jaw's front panel.

Still writing ribcage geometry...

I'll skip fingers and hand details, adding a few scattered loose boxes for vertebrae instead, then move to finalizing the code — making sure all my helper functions and types actually get used so nothing is flagged as unused. I also need to watch out for a TypeScript issue: spreading a number array into a Vector3 constructor won't type-check as a tuple, so I'll construct Vector3 directly instead.

I'm working out a merge helper that combines multiple box geometries into one BufferGeometry, handling the null-check since mergeGeometries can return null, and I need to keep attribute types consistent across boxes. For rotated rivet geometry like the chest pieces, I'm transforming each box's geometry by rotating and translating it into world coordinates before merging.
